question: What are the primary differences between Creo Object TOOLKIT (OTK) C++ and legacy Pro/TOOLKIT (C API)?
answer:
Creo Object TOOLKIT (OTK) C++ and Pro/TOOLKIT (C API) represent two distinct generations of PTC's CAD customization architecture.

Feature / AspectPro/TOOLKIT (C API)Object TOOLKIT (OTK C++)
Programming ParadigmProcedural C API relying on flat function prefixes (Pro*).Modern Object-Oriented C++ with structured namespaces (pfc*, wfc*).
Memory ManagementManual allocation/freeing (ProArrayAlloc, ProArrayFree, ProWstringFree).RAII and smart-pointer reference counted handles (automatic garbage prevention).
Feature ModelingHeavily dependent on Element Trees (ProElement) for definition.Object-oriented model entities and feature operations with cleaner abstractions.
PerformanceDirect DLL execution; very fast, but requires significant boilerplate.Native C++ speed with expressive syntax and lower maintenance cost.
CompatibilityDeep legacy coverage across all Creo versions back to Pro/ENGINEER.Standard choice for all modern PTC development and enterprise plugins.

Verdict: Choose OTK C++ for new enterprise applications, while retaining Pro/TOOLKIT knowledge for lower-level element tree manipulations.

question: What is the purpose of the protk.dat file and what are its mandatory parameters?
answer:
The protk.dat file is the registry configuration file that dictates how and when Creo Parametric loads custom external plugins.

Key Mandatory and Common Parameters:

  • NAME: The internal unique logical identifier for the application.
  • EXEC_PATH: Absolute or environment-variable resolved path to the compiled executable or DLL.
  • TEXT_DIR: Absolute path to the folder containing UI dialog definitions, message catalogs (.txt), and icons.
  • STARTUP: Load mechanism — typically dll (loaded inside Creo address space) or spawn (external asynchronous process).
  • ALLOW_STOP: Set to TRUE or FALSE to allow/prohibit the user from manually stopping the plugin from the Creo Aux Applications menu.
  • REVISION: Version string verifying Creo compatibility (e.g., Creo Parametric 9.0).

Example protk.dat:

NAME        CustomExportApp
EXEC_PATH   C:\CreoPlugins\bin\CustomExportApp.dll
TEXT_DIR    C:\CreoPlugins\text
STARTUP     dll
ALLOW_STOP  TRUE
REVISION    Creo 8.0
END

question: Differentiate between Synchronous and Asynchronous execution modes in Creo Toolkit.
answer:
Creo automation supports two execution architectures depending on whether the code runs inside or outside Creo's process:

  • Synchronous Mode (In-Process DLL):
    • The custom program is compiled as a dynamic library (.dll) loaded directly into Creo's memory space.
    • Executed via ribbon buttons, menu triggers, or notification hooks.
    • Creo halts user interaction while your API callback runs, providing maximum throughput and low-latency memory access.
  • Asynchronous Mode (Out-of-Process EXE):
    • The custom program runs as an independent executable process (.exe), communicating with Creo via RPC/socket protocols.
    • Can launch Creo Parametric invisibly in batch mode or connect to an already active session via ProSessionConnect().
    • Essential for batch file translators, CAD workers, automated drawing dispatchers, and PLM background services.

question: How do you traverse and iterate over all features in a solid model using Pro/TOOLKIT?
answer:
In Pro/TOOLKIT, object traversal adheres to the Visitor Callback Pattern using the ProSolidFeatVisit() API.

Traversing Steps:

  1. Obtain the current solid model handle (ProSolid or ProMdl).
  2. Implement a filter function (ProFeatureFilterAction) to skip unwanted features (e.g., internal/suppressed).
  3. Implement an action function (ProFeatureVisitAction) to execute logic on matching items.
  4. Invoke ProSolidFeatVisit() passing the function pointers and user data context.

C Implementation:

ProError FeatureFilter(ProFeature* p_feat, ProAppData app_data) {
    ProFeattype type;
    ProFeatureTypeGet(p_feat, &type);
    return (type == PRO_FEAT_HOLE) ? PRO_TK_NO_ERROR : PRO_TK_CONTINUE;
}

ProError FeatureVisit(ProFeature* p_feat, ProError status, ProAppData app_data) {
    // Process each hole feature
    return PRO_TK_NO_ERROR; // PRO_TK_USER_ABORT halts traversal
}

question: Explain the concept of an Element Tree (ProElement) when creating features programmatically.
answer:
An Element Tree is a structured hierarchical container describing all geometric parameters, references, tolerances, section references, and operational flags needed to construct a CAD feature.

Core Workflow:

  • Root Initialization: Call ProElemtreeCreate() to create the empty container.
  • Node Allocation: Allocate element nodes using ProElementAlloc() with predefined element IDs (e.g., PRO_E_STD_FEATURE_NAME, PRO_E_EXT_DEPTH).
  • Value Assignment: Set values using ProElementValSet() (supporting values like integers, doubles, wide strings, and selection references).
  • Tree Assembly: Call ProElemtreeElementAdd() to form compound hierarchical sub-trees.
  • Feature Generation: Pass the completed root tree to ProFeatureCreate().
  • Memory Cleanup: Call ProElementFree() to release the allocated tree memory.

question: Explain the distinction between ProMdl, ProSolid, ProPart, and ProAssembly handles in Creo Toolkit.
answer:
Creo's C API uses opaque pointer types with a strict conceptual hierarchy:

Handle TypeScope & RepresentationApplicable Functions
ProMdlGeneric model handle representing any Creo file type (Part, Assembly, Drawing, Section).ProMdlCurrentGet, ProMdlSave, ProMdlErase, ProMdlNameGet.
ProSolidSubtype of ProMdl representing models with 3D solid geometry (Parts and Assemblies).ProSolidFeatVisit, ProSolidRegenerate, ProSolidMassPropertyGet.
ProPartSpecialized handle representing specifically a .prt solid part.ProPartSurfVisit, ProPartMaterialCurrentGet.
ProAssemblySpecialized handle representing specifically an .asm assembly structure.ProAssemblyComponentAdd, ProAssemblyExplodedViewGet.

Casting Principle: Because ProSolid, ProPart, and ProAssembly are type-compatible with ProMdl, you can safely cast them to ProMdl for generic session operations.

question: What is the difference between File -> Erase and File -> Delete in Creo, and what are their API equivalents?
answer:
Understanding the difference between memory space and disk storage is critical in CAD customization:

  • File -> Erase:
    • Removes the model from Creo's active working memory (RAM / in-session cache).
    • Leaves the physical file on the local hard disk or Windchill vault completely intact.
    • API Equivalent: ProMdlErase() or ProMdlEraseAll(). Erasing requires that no active dependencies or open windows reference the model.
  • File -> Delete:
    • Purges specific versions or all iterations of the physical file directly from the local disk/directory.
    • API Equivalent: ProFileDelete() or standard OS file removal APIs.

Safety Warning: When doing automated batch runs, always call ProMdlErase() after saving and exporting to prevent the Creo session from exhausting system RAM.

question: How do you programmatically create, read, and modify a model parameter, and designate it to Windchill?
answer:
Model parameters are managed through the ProParameter* API suite.

Step-by-Step Implementation:

  1. Creation: Initialize a ProModelitem representing the model, initialize a ProParamvalue union, and call:
    ProParameterCreate(&model_item, L"PART_NUMBER", &value, ¶m);
  2. Reading: Call ProParameterInit(&model_item, L"PART_NUMBER", ¶m) followed by ProParameterValueGet(¶m, &value).
  3. Modifying: Update the value using ProParameterValueSet(¶m, &new_value).
  4. Windchill Designation: Use ProParameterDesignationSet(¶m, PRO_B_TRUE) to mark the parameter for automatic metadata synchronization to Windchill attributes.

Code Snippet:

ProParameter param;
ProParamvalue val;
val.type = PRO_PARAM_STRING;
ProWstringCopy(L"ENG-2026-X", val.value.s_val, PRO_VALUE_UNUSED);
ProParameterCreate((ProModelitem*)&solid, L"DRAWING_REF", &val, ¶m);
ProParameterDesignationSet(¶m, PRO_B_TRUE);

question: What are Trail files in Creo/ProE, and how can they be utilized or mitigated in automation testing?
answer:
A Trail file (e.g., trail.txt.*) is an internal deterministic journal logging every user interaction, coordinate pick, string typed, ribbon action, and API call during a Creo session.

Role in Automation & Development:

  • Crash Forensics: When custom code causes an access violation (SEH crash), the trail file shows the exact sequence of commands and coordinate picks leading up to the fault.
  • Automated Regression Testing: Trail files can be replayed from the command line (creo.exe -trail file.txt) to reproduce automated smoke tests without human intervention.
  • Mitigation in Batch Processing: Continuous batch processing can generate thousands of trail files. Developers configure trail_dir in config.pro to direct trail files to a temporary scrap directory and auto-purge them post-execution.

question: How do you programmatically add and solve Relations in a Creo part or assembly?
answer:
Relations are mathematical formulas and conditional statements governing parametric dimensions and parameters.

Key APIs & Execution Pattern:

  • ProRelationGet(ProModelitem* item, ProRelset* relset): Retrieves the collection of relation statements currently attached to a part, assembly, or feature.
  • ProRelationSet(ProModelitem* item, ProRelset* relset): Assigns a list of wide-string statements to the target object.
  • ProSolidRegenerate(ProSolid solid, PRO_REGEN_FORCE): Forces evaluation of the mathematical solver against the active model.

Example Relation String Array:

ProWstring relations[2] = {
    L"D1 = LENGTH * 2.5",
    L"IF WIDTH > 50 
 D2 = 10 
 ELSE 
 D2 = 5 
 ENDIF"
};

Best Practice: Check dimensions and referenced parameter names before setting relations to prevent regeneration lockups.

question: Explain the B-Rep (Boundary Representation) topology hierarchy in Creo and how to navigate it via the API.
answer:
Creo represents 3D solid geometry through a hierarchical Boundary Representation (B-Rep) topological model.

Hierarchy Flow:

  • ProSolid → Contains features and geometric roots.
  • ProSurface → Bounded 3D geometric surfaces (planes, cylinders, B-splines). Accessed via ProSolidSurfaceVisit().
  • ProQuilt → Stitched composite collection of surfaces.
  • ProContour → Closed bounding loop of edges defining the boundary of a surface (outer boundary vs internal cutouts/holes).
  • ProEdge → 1D topological boundary curve shared between two adjacent surfaces.
  • ProPoint / ProVertex → 0D endpoints of edges.

Navigation Pattern:

Start at a surface, invoke ProSurfaceContourVisit() to traverse its contours, and call ProContourEdgeVisit() to extract the shared bounding edges.

question: What is a ProSelection object and how is it constructed programmatically without user UI interaction?
answer:
A ProSelection is a smart handle representing a reference to a geometric item or feature, including its topological context and assembly transform path.

Programmatic Construction (Without GUI Prompt):

  1. Single Part Context: Use ProSelectionAlloc() with a ProModelitem (such as a ProSurface or ProGeomitem):
    ProSelectionAlloc(NULL, &geom_item, &p_selection);
  2. Assembly Occurrence Context: When picking geometry inside a nested subassembly, pass the valid ProAsmcomppath as the first argument so Creo understands the spatial transformation matrix:
    ProSelectionAlloc(&comp_path, &geom_item, &p_selection);

Crucial Rule: Programmatically allocated selections allocate memory and must always be freed with ProSelectionFree(&p_selection).

question: How are Assembly Component Paths (ProAsmcomppath) used when working with nested assemblies?
answer:
When an identical part exists in multiple locations within a complex assembly tree, Creo needs a coordinate transform trail called a ProAsmcomppath.

Structure Definition:

typedef struct pro_asm_comp_path {
    ProSolid   owner;         // Top-level assembly
    ProIdTable comp_id_table; // Array of component feature IDs down the tree
    int        table_num;     // Depth count of nested components
} ProAsmcomppath;

Key Capabilities:

  • Transformation Matrix: ProAsmcomppathTrfGet() calculates the 4x4 coordinate transform matrix between the top-level assembly and the localized part coordinate system.
  • Disambiguation: Allows querying face measurements, interference, or adding drawing dimensions to a specific part instance rather than all occurrences.

question: Explain the process of programmatically assembling a component into an assembly using constraints.
answer:
Assembling a component programmatically requires creating an assembly component feature and defining mathematical constraint pairs.

Step-by-Step Procedure:

  1. Create Component Occurrence: Use ProAssemblyComponentAdd(assembly, part_mdl, &comp_feat).
  2. Initialize Element Tree: Call ProElementAlloc() for PRO_E_COMPONENT_CONSTRAINTS.
  3. Define Constraint Pairs: Add sub-elements for constraint type (PRO_ASM_MATE, PRO_ASM_ALIGN, PRO_ASM_INSERT, or PRO_ASM_CSYS).
  4. Assign References: Provide pairs of ProSelection objects — one from the target component and one from the parent assembly.
  5. Redefine Feature: Call ProFeatureElemtreeSet() or ProFeatureCreate() to enforce the constraint solver.
  6. Regenerate: Invoke ProSolidRegenerate() to settle physical component positions.

question: What are Component Interfaces in Creo and how can they be leveraged in automation?
answer:
Component Interfaces are predefined sets of assembly mating conditions, references, and rules saved directly inside a part or subassembly model (e.g., standard fasteners with predefined insert and mate references).

Advantages in Automation:

  • Zero Guesswork: Automation scripts do not need to hunt for surface names or calculate bounding planes on every run.
  • Rapid Auto-Assembly: The Toolkit API can invoke ProAssemblyComponentAutoplace() to snap the component into a matching interface in the parent assembly in a single call.
  • Stability: Insulates automation code from geometry renumbering and topological name changes.

question: How do you automate Family Tables in Creo using Pro/TOOLKIT?
answer:
A Family Table is an internal matrix of generic CAD templates driving multiple standardized instances via parameters, dimensions, and suppressed/resumed features.

API Workflow:

  • Iteration: Call ProFamtableRowVisit() and ProFamtableColVisit() to traverse instances (rows) and driving members/parameters (columns).
  • Add New Instance: Use ProFaminstanceAdd(famtable, L"INSTANCE_NAME").
  • Set Instance Values: Call ProFaminstanceValueEdit() to set cell values for specific parameters or dimension tags.
  • Verification: Call ProFaminstanceVerify() to programmatically build the instance in memory and verify regeneration without model errors.
  • Retrieval: Call ProFaminstanceRetrieve() to load the generated specific part instance into session as a distinct ProSolid.

question: How can you programmatically export models to neutral formats like STEP, IGES, DXF, and PDF?
answer:
Exporting models is standard in PLM CAD worker automations. Creo provides specialized output instructions per format.

Implementation Strategy:

  • 3D Neutral Formats (STEP / IGES): Initialize a ProStepOutputFileFormat or ProIgesOutputFileFormat struct, configure coordinate systems and options via ProStepExport() or ProOutputFileWrite().
  • 2D Drawings to PDF: Use ProPDFoptionsAlloc(), configure DPI, stroke widths, color depth, and sheets, then call ProPDFExport().
  • Drawings to DXF: Use ProDrawingDxfExport() using a mapped dxf_export.pro configuration file for layer mapping.

Sample PDF Export:

ProPDFoptions pdf_opts;
ProPDFoptionsAlloc(&pdf_opts);
ProPDFoptionsColorDepthSet(pdf_opts, PRO_PDF_CD_COLOR);
ProPDFExport(drawing, pdf_opts, L"C:\\exports\\output.pdf");
ProPDFoptionsFree(pdf_opts);

question: What is the proper method to handle memory allocation and prevent leaks with ProArray in Pro/TOOLKIT?
answer:
In Pro/TOOLKIT C API, variable-length lists use an opaque heap structure called ProArray.

Lifecycle Management:

  • Allocation: Allocated with ProArrayAlloc(size, sizeof(Type), growth_step, (ProArray*)&array).
  • Size Tracking: The count of active elements is queried with ProArraySizeGet(array, &size).
  • Appending: Dynamic expansion is achieved via ProArrayObjectAdd().
  • Deallocation: You MUST call ProArrayFree((ProArray*)&array) once execution concludes.

Common Defect: Many API functions (like ProSolidSurfaceVisit or ProFeatureGeomitemVisit collecting into an array) allocate array memory on the heap inside the API. Failing to call ProArrayFree() on return causes cumulative memory leaks that crash batch sessions.

question: Explain wide string handling (wchar_t / ProWstring) and conversions in Creo Toolkit.
answer:
Creo internally utilizes two-byte wide Unicode character buffers (wchar_t* / ProWstring) to support multi-language localizations (Japanese, German, Chinese, etc.).

Conversion Patterns:

  • ASCII/UTF-8 to ProWstring: ProStringToWstring(p_wstring, char_string).
  • ProWstring to ASCII/UTF-8: ProWstringToString(char_string, p_wstring).
  • String Copy: ProWstringCopy(source, target, PRO_VALUE_UNUSED).
  • String Comparison: ProWstringCompare(str1, str2, PRO_VALUE_UNUSED).

Security Warning: Always ensure target wchar arrays have double the allocated byte size or use PRO_NAME_SIZE / PRO_PATH_SIZE constants to avoid buffer overflows.

question: What are Notification Handlers (ProNotificationSet) and what are their typical use cases?
answer:
Notification Handlers are event listener callbacks that register user code to execute automatically in response to internal Creo life-cycle events.

Signature: ProNotificationSet(ProNotifyType notify_type, ProNotifyFunction func)

Common Notification Events:

  • PRO_MDL_RETRIEVE_POST: Fires immediately after a model finishes loading. Ideal for validating corporate standards.
  • PRO_MDL_SAVE_PRE: Triggered right before saving to disk. Used to enforce parameter verification, naming conventions, and layer cleanups.
  • PRO_SOLID_REGEN_POST: Fires after regeneration. Used to update computed metadata or check design limits.
  • PRO_SESSION_EXIT: Clean up auxiliary database handles and network sockets before Creo closes.

question: How do you automate Drawing Sheet creation, view scaling, and layout configuration?
answer:
Drawing automation utilizes the ProDrawing* API family:

  1. Sheet Operations:
    • Add sheets via ProDrawingSheetCreate(drawing, &sheet_id).
    • Set active sheet using ProDrawingCurrentSheetSet(drawing, sheet_id).
    • Apply standard format borders using ProDrawingFormatAdd(drawing, sheet_id, format_mdl).
  2. View Creation:
    • Create a general or projection view using ProDrawingGeneralviewCreate() or ProDrawingProjectedviewCreate().
    • Define the 3D model orientation vector and place the 2D view point coordinates via ProPoint3d.
    • Set view scale using ProDrawingViewScaleSet(drawing, view, scale).
  3. Update Display: Call ProDrawingViewsRegenerate() followed by ProDrawingDisplay().

question: How do you automate Bill of Materials (BOM) creation and Repeat Regions in Creo drawings?
answer:
BOM tables in Creo drawings are constructed using Tables populated with Repeat Region report symbols.

Automation Sequence:

  1. Table Placement: Call ProDrawingTableCreate(drawing, &table_data, display_flag, &table).
  2. Repeat Region Definition: Define row boundaries as dynamic using ProDrawingTableRegionAdd().
  3. Report Symbol Ingestion: Populate header and repeat cells with evaluation strings:
    • asm.mbr.name → Component model name.
    • rpt.qty → Evaluated component quantity.
    • asm.mbr.param_name → Custom Windchill parameters (e.g., Description, Material).
  4. Table Update: Execute ProDrawingTablesUpdate() to invoke the BOM engine, automatically populating rows matching the assembly structure.

question: Explain how to programmatically attach Notes and Dimensions to drawing views.
answer:
Annotations and notes are bound to drawing sheets using the ProAnnotation and ProDrawing* APIs.

Attaching a Drawing Note:

  1. Create a note descriptor using ProDrawingNoteCreate().
  2. Define the text array containing wide string lines.
  3. Set attachment properties using ProNoteAttachAlloc() — configuring either on-item attachment (leader pointing to an edge/surface) or free floating with screen coordinates.

Showing Model Dimensions:

Rather than synthesizing drafting dimensions, best practice is to query model dimensions via ProSolidDimensionVisit() and toggle their visibility in the drawing view using ProDimensionShow(dim, view, drawing), ensuring geometric associativity.

question: How does Ribbon and UI customization work in Creo Parametric using XML and Toolkit callbacks?
answer:
Creo modern Ribbon customization pairs custom XML interface definitions with Toolkit action bindings.

Architecture Layers:

  1. Ribbon Definition: A creo_ribbon_customization.xml file defines tabs, groups, buttons, and flyouts along with their icons and help tooltips.
  2. Command Registration: In the plugin initialization (user_initialize()), register custom commands using:
    ProCmdActionAdd("CustomCmd_ACT", ActionCallback, uiProeImmediate, AccessCallback, PRO_B_FALSE, PRO_B_FALSE, &cmd_id);
  3. Action Callback: Executes the functional automation logic when clicked.
  4. Access Callback: Evaluates context (e.g., returns PRO_TK_ACCESS_AVAILABLE if a Part model is active, or PRO_TK_ACCESS_UNAVAILABLE if no window is open) to enable or gray-out the button.

question: What is the ProUI dialog engine and how does it compare to native Windows GUI frameworks (MFC/Qt/WPF)?
answer:
ProUI is PTC's embedded platform-independent dialog description framework.

FeatureProUIMFC / Qt / WPF
Look and FeelNative to Creo; identical styling, dark/light theme tracking.External OS window style; requires manual theme syncing.
DefinitionDefined via .res resource files in the text directory.Defined via Qt .ui, XAML, or Visual Studio resource dialogs.
Event LoopManaged inside Creo main thread via ProUIDialogCreate().Requires modal event loop hooking or non-modal threading controls.
MaintenanceGuaranteed cross-version UI compatibility.Risk of window handle conflicts or docking incompatibilities.

Recommendation: Use ProUI for simple modals and parameter editors; use Qt or WPF for sophisticated web-like, dashboard, or heavy data-grid applications.

question: What are the common ProError status codes in Pro/TOOLKIT and how should errors be logged and handled?
answer:
Almost every Pro/TOOLKIT function returns an enum value of type ProError indicating execution status.

Critical ProError Codes:

  • PRO_TK_NO_ERROR (0): Function completed successfully.
  • PRO_TK_BAD_INPUTS (-1): Passed invalid pointer, NULL reference, or out-of-range argument.
  • PRO_TK_NOT_FOUND (-4): Specified parameter, feature, coordinate system, or file does not exist.
  • PRO_TK_GENERAL_ERROR (-2): Broad failure such as a regeneration error or locked database.
  • PRO_TK_CANT_MODIFY (-13): Target feature is read-only, locked by Windchill, or suppressed.
  • PRO_TK_USER_ABORT (-9): Return code used within visitors to gracefully exit loops.

Engineering Standard: Always enclose Toolkit calls with an error assertion macro that logs line number, function name, and status code to an external diagnostic log file.

question: How do you execute headless batch operations without loading the graphical user interface?
answer:
Running batch automations (e.g., converting 10,000 models to STEP overnight) requires suppressing UI rendering overhead.

Techniques:

  • Asynchronous Non-Graphics Mode: When calling ProSessionStart(), pass the commandline flag -nogbi (No Graphic Bus Interface) or -batch.
  • Suppress Display Calls: Never invoke ProMdlDisplay() or ProWindowActivate() during processing loops.
  • Memory Erase Hygiene: Perform:
    ProMdlSave(mdl); ProMdlErase(mdl); ProDirectoryCurrentSet(); to clear memory after processing each part.
  • Window Management: If operating inside a synchronous plugin, keep the active window minimised and avoid redrawing the model tree.

Gain: Performance increases by 4x to 8x compared to interactive sessions.

question: Explain the role and architecture of Skeleton Models in Top-Down assembly design automation.
answer:
A Skeleton Model (.skel) is a specialized assembly component used in Top-Down Design to establish geometric references, motion limits, space envelopes, and critical interfaces before detailing components.

Automation Architecture:

  • Single Source of Truth: The automation script modifies parameters and dimensions only on the skeleton model.
  • Geometry Publication & Copy: Features in child parts reference the skeleton via Publish Geometry and External Copy Geometry features.
  • Robust Regeneration: Because child parts consume published skeleton surfaces, component regeneration doesn't trigger circular parent-child dependency loops.
  • API Handling: Identified in Toolkit via ProAsmcompMdlNameGet() with type PRO_MDL_SKELETON.

question: How do you detect and resolve circular references in assembly models programmatically?
answer:
A Circular Reference occurs when Component A depends on Component B, while Component B indirectly references Component A, destabilizing regeneration loops.

Detection & Resolution via API:

  • Reference Investigation: Call ProFeatureDependenciesGet() or ProReferenceOwnerGet() to construct an in-memory directed acyclic dependency graph (DAG).
  • Cycle Detection: Apply graph cycle-detection algorithms (e.g., Tarjan's or DFS) across parent-child links.
  • External Dependency Flags: Read config.pro setting ref_scope_violations to alert on external links out of assembly scope.
  • Remediation: Break dynamic external reference loops by freezing references or rerouting them to a centralized skeleton geometry publish feature.

question: How do you integrate Creo Toolkit applications with PTC Windchill PLM?
answer:
Creo communicates natively with Windchill through the embedded browser and the ProServer API module.

Primary Integration Workflows:

  • Workspace Management: Use ProServerWorkspaceGet() and ProServerWorkspaceRegister() to query the active Windchill sandbox workspace.
  • Checkout / Checkin Automation: Initiate automated checkouts before programmatic modification via ProServerObjectsCheckout() and checkin with metadata via ProServerObjectsCheckin().
  • Windchill Attributes: Synchronize CAD parameters with Windchill Soft Type attributes using designated ProParameterDesignationSet().
  • CAD Worker / Worker Daemon: Custom toolkit plugins are deployed on Windchill conversion servers to auto-publish thumbnails, visual 3D representations (PVZ), and standard neutral CAD files upon check-in.

question: What is the difference between J-Link, Creo Parametric WEB.LINK, and VB API?
answer:
Beyond C++ Toolkit, PTC historically supported multiple rapid application scripting APIs:

TechnologyLanguageExecution ContextTypical Use Case
J-LinkJavaRuns in Creo's embedded JVM.Platform-independent UI utilities, quick dialog tools (deprecated in favor of OTK Java).
WEB.LINKJavaScriptRuns inside Creo's embedded Chromium browser.Intranet portals, custom model catalogs, HTML-driven part selection forms.
VB APIVB.NET / COMRuns as external Windows COM automation.Integration with Microsoft Office, Excel macro-driven design calculators.

Modern Trend: Modern architectures standardize on OTK C++ for performance or OTK Python / Java for higher productivity.

question: How do you extract physical Mass Properties (weight, center of gravity, moments of inertia) using the API?
answer:
Mass properties extraction is critical for structural validation and automated engineering compliance reporting.

Implementation Steps:

  1. Verify density and material assignment via ProMaterialCurrentGet().
  2. Initialize a ProMassProperty container struct.
  3. Call ProSolidMassPropertyGet(solid, NULL, &mass_prop).
  4. Read the populated physical values:
    • mass_prop.mass: Total calculated mass.
    • mass_prop.volume & mass_prop.surface_area: Geometric volumes.
    • mass_prop.center_of_gravity: 3D coordinates relative to default CSYS.
    • mass_prop.inertia_tensor: Moments of inertia matrix.

question: How do you programmatically configure and switch Simplified Reps (Representations) in large assemblies?
answer:
Simplified Representations (Simp Reps) drastically cut RAM consumption and acceleration latency by loading only required components in large assemblies.

API Workflow:

  • Query Reps: Traverse existing representations using ProAssemblySimprepVisit().
  • Activate Rep: Call ProSimprepActivate(assembly, &simprep) to dynamically swap active geometry.
  • Create Custom Rep: Use ProSimprepCreate() and add component rules:
    • PRO_SIMPREP_EXCLUDE: Removes geometry and child parts completely from RAM.
    • PRO_SIMPREP_GRAPHICS: Loads display tessellation without parametric feature trees.
    • PRO_SIMPREP_GEOMETRY: Loads accurate surface boundary geometry without feature history.

question: Explain how to debug a Creo Toolkit application in Visual Studio using live process attachment.
answer:
Because Creo plugins execute within xtop.exe (the core Creo executable engine), developers debug synchronous plugins via process attachment.

Debugging Procedure:

  1. Compile the DLL with full Debug Information (/Zi compiler flag) and generate .pdb symbol files.
  2. Launch Creo Parametric independently.
  3. Open the custom plugin solution in Visual Studio.
  4. Navigate to Debug → Attach to Process..., locate xtop.exe, and attach with Native code debugging.
  5. Set breakpoints inside Toolkit action handlers.
  6. In Creo, trigger the ribbon command; Visual Studio halts execution at the breakpoint with complete call stack and variable inspection.

question: What are User Defined Features (UDFs) and how can they be placed programmatically?
answer:
A User Defined Feature (UDF) (.gph file) is a group of preconfigured parametric features packaged together for recurring use (e.g., standardized mounting bosses, keyways, or electrical ports).

Automation Workflow:

  1. Load UDF Definition: Call ProUdfread() pointing to the .gph file path.
  2. Map Prompt References: Query required reference prompts using ProUdfdataPromptsGet() and assign matching ProSelection handles (e.g., placement surfaces, alignment datums).
  3. Set Variable Dimensions: Supply dimension values or variable parameters using ProUdfdataDimvaluesSet().
  4. Instantiate: Execute ProUdfCreate() to construct the UDF group in the target model tree.

question: How do you programmatically manipulate Layers and control entity visibility in Creo?
answer:
Layers organize model and drawing items (datums, sketches, surfaces, annotations) to control screen clarity and corporate compliance standards.

Layer Automation APIs:

  • Layer Iteration: ProSolidLayerVisit() iterates through all defined layers.
  • Layer Creation: ProLayerCreate(solid, L"3D_DATUM_PLANES", &layer) creates a missing standard layer.
  • Add Items: Call ProLayerItemAdd(&layer, &model_item) to assign datum axes, planes, or coordinates.
  • Display State Control: Use ProLayerDisplaystatusSet(&layer, PRO_LAYER_BLANK) to hide entities, or PRO_LAYER_DISPLAY to show them.
  • Save Status: Invoke ProLayerDisplaystatusSave() to persist visibility settings into the model file.

question: Explain the concept of Feature Regeneration and how to handle Regeneration Failures in automated code.
answer:
Regeneration is Creo's algorithmic recompilation of geometric topology according to feature trees, parent-child references, and dimension solvers.

API Strategy & Failure Mitigation:

  • Invoking Regeneration: Call ProSolidRegenerate(solid, PRO_REGEN_FORCE).
  • Error Detection: If the model enters a failed state, the function returns non-zero error codes such as PRO_TK_GENERAL_ERROR.
  • Diagnosing Failed Features: Traverse features with ProSolidFeatVisit() and inspect their status with ProFeatureStatusGet() checking for PRO_FEAT_UNREGENERATED or PRO_FEAT_FAILED.
  • Rollback Strategy: Programmatically catch failures and execute ProFeatureSuppress(), revert the offending parameter, or perform ProMdlErase() without saving to protect production models from corruption.

question: How can you programmatically control Session Windows, Active Views, and Screen Refreshing?
answer:
Controlling active graphics windows is necessary when switching between parts, assemblies, and drawing canvases.

API Workflow:

  • Window Retrieval: Call ProWindowCurrentGet(&window_id) to identify active viewport.
  • Window Association: Use ProObjectwindowCreate(model_name, type, &window_id) to initialize a dedicated viewport for a background model.
  • Activation: Switch focus using ProWindowActivate(window_id).
  • Repainting: Redraw graphics explicitly via ProWindowRepaint(window_id).
  • Screen Freeze: To eliminate visual flickering and accelerate loops, invoke ProGraphicsUnHighlight() and refrain from calling window activation until all batch operations conclude.

question: How do you detect geometric collisions and calculate clearance/interference between components in an assembly?
answer:
Automated assembly interference checks eliminate costly tooling clashes and packaging interferences.

API Mechanisms:

  • Pairwise Interference: Call ProAssemblyInterferenceCompute() passing two component selections to evaluate whether their solid bodies intersect.
  • Volume Analysis: The API returns a ProInterferenceData structure containing total intersection volume and collision contact curves.
  • Global Assembly Scan: Traverse pairs with ProSolidFeatVisit() or invoke global clearance checking using ProAssemblyClearanceCompute() to ensure minimum design offsets (e.g., minimum 5.0mm clearance between wiring harness and engine housing).

question: What is the config.pro file, and how can configuration settings be queried or altered dynamically at runtime?
answer:
config.pro is Creo's configuration master file containing operational switches, corporate drafting standards, directory locations, and mapkeys.

Runtime Manipulation via Toolkit:

  • Querying an Option: Call ProConfigoptGet(L"template_solidpart", val_string) to read active corporate settings.
  • Setting an Option Dynamically: Call ProConfigoptSet(L"drawing_setup_file", L"C:\\standards\\iso.dtl") to alter configuration during session execution without requiring a restart.
  • Mapkey Injection: Dynamic mapkeys can be synthesized and fed directly to the Creo input queue using ProMacroExecute().

question: How do you create and manage Coordinate Systems (CSYS) programmatically in Creo Toolkit?
answer:
Coordinate systems serve as reference origins for manufacturing fixtures, inspection planes, and assembly offsets.

Creation Steps via Element Tree:

  1. Allocate element tree with PRO_E_FEATURE_TYPE set to PRO_FEAT_CSYS.
  2. Define the origin reference (a 3D vertex, datum point, or intersecting planes) in PRO_E_CSYS_ORIGIN_CONSTR.
  3. Define Axis Orientation: Set X, Y, and Z vector alignments pointing to planar surfaces or datum axes.
  4. Commit the definition using ProFeatureCreate().
  5. Extraction: For existing models, call ProGeomitemToCsys() and ProCsysTransformGet() to obtain the 4x4 orientation matrix relative to the global world origin.

question: What are Mapkeys in Creo, and what are their limitations compared to Toolkit development?
answer:
A Mapkey is a recorded keyboard macro executing a hardcoded sequence of UI clicks, ribbon selections, and text entries.

AspectMapkey MacroToolkit / OTK API
ComplexityLimited to linear, predefined click playback.Full programming logic (conditional branching, loops, external SQL/REST APIs).
Error HandlingFragile; halts abruptly if a dialog prompt slightly differs or changes.Enterprise error codes (ProError), try/catch recovery, diagnostics logging.
PerformanceSlow UI playback; redraws every intermediary step.Direct in-memory manipulation without rendering delays.
Data ExtractionCannot calculate matrices or inspect B-Rep topology.Complete programmatic access to math models, geometry, and PLM.

Conclusion: Mapkeys are quick solutions for personal desktop shortcuts; Toolkit is essential for robust, mission-critical enterprise engineering pipelines.

question: How do you programmatically assign and manage Materials in Creo parts?
answer:
Material assignments dictate structural mass properties, FEA simulations, and BOM manufacturing attributes.

Material Automation Pattern:

  1. Load Material: Read a corporate material definition file (.mtl) using ProPartMaterialLoad(part, L"ALUMINUM_6061_T6").
  2. Set Active Material: Assign the active material via ProPartMaterialCurrentSet(part, L"ALUMINUM_6061_T6").
  3. Inspect Parameters: Retrieve material properties (Young's Modulus, Poisson's ratio, Thermal Conductivity) through ProMaterialPropertyGet().
  4. Delete / Purge: Remove unused legacy material definitions using ProPartMaterialDelete() to keep model data clean.

question: What is the difference between Model Items (ProModelitem) and Geometric Items (ProGeomitem)?
answer:
Understanding the distinction between logical features and physical geometry entities is foundational in Creo customization:

  • ProModelitem: The generic base structure representing any logical entity in the model tree. This includes features, parameters, layers, views, dimensions, and coordinate systems. Holds type, id, and owner.
  • ProGeomitem: A specific subclass of ProModelitem representing concrete geometric entities generated by features. Examples include surfaces (PRO_SURFACE), edges (PRO_EDGE), datum axes (PRO_AXIS), and datum planes.

Conversion: You can convert a generic geometric item handle to a specialized surface handle using ProGeomitemToSurface(&geom_item, &surface).

question: How do you programmatically package and license a custom Creo Toolkit application?
answer:
PTC governs third-party toolkit execution through license authentication locks.

Licensing & Unlocking Flow:

  • Compilation & Build: Applications compile with the Creo Toolkit headers and link against protk.lib or OTK libraries.
  • Toolkit Licensing (protk_unlock): Historically, standalone C applications required running PTC's unlock utility (protk_unlock.exe my_plugin.dll) using an authorized PTC development license to remove development watermark limits.
  • Modern Creo Licensing: Modern OTK builds check for optional modules (e.g., Creo Parametric TOOLKIT API license) at runtime during user_initialize(). If licensing fails, the plugin unloads cleanly to prevent Creo session failure.

question: How do you execute transactions and atomic operations to roll back changes upon failure in Creo Toolkit?
answer:
CAD automation requires robust transaction management to prevent half-finished modifications from corrupting engineering databases.

Transaction Architecture:

  1. Session Backup / Copy: Before initiating complex multi-feature alterations, perform an in-memory duplicate using ProMdlBackup() or save an iteration mark.
  2. Transaction Boundary: Execute modifications within an explicit logic block.
  3. Validation Check: Trigger a trial regeneration via ProSolidRegenerate().
  4. Rollback Mechanism: If any step returns PRO_TK_GENERAL_ERROR:
    • Call ProFeatureDelete() or ProFeatureSuppress() on newly instantiated elements.
    • Alternatively, erase the memory model using ProMdlErase() and reload the original clean iteration from disk or Windchill cache.

question: Explain how to traverse an Assembly BOM structure hierarchically using recursive API visitation.
answer:
Traversing an entire assembly hierarchy down to raw piece parts requires a recursive visitor function.

Implementation Strategy:

  1. Define a recursive function TraverseAssembly(ProAssembly asm, int depth).
  2. Use ProSolidFeatVisit() filtering specifically for component features (PRO_FEAT_COMPONENT).
  3. Within the visitor callback, query the underlying model handle using ProAsmcompMdlGet().
  4. Inspect the model type via ProMdlTypeGet():
    • If PRO_MDL_PART: Process part metadata, quantity counts, and finish parameters.
    • If PRO_MDL_ASSEMBLY: Increment tree depth, format indentations, and recursively call TraverseAssembly() on the child subassembly.

question: What is the difference between Feature Suppression and Feature Deletion in automation, and when should each be used?
answer:
Managing model lifecycle requires distinguishing between temporary suppression and permanent deletion:

  • ProFeatureSuppress():
    • Temporarily suspends the feature from memory and active regeneration calculations.
    • Retains the feature element definition in the model tree.
    • Advantage: Can be resurrected anytime using ProFeatureResume(). Essential for dynamic Family Tables and configurable product variants.
  • ProFeatureDelete():
    • Permanently destroys the feature and eradicates it from the CAD database.
    • Cascades destructively to all children features unless children are rerouted or deleted in clip mode.
    • Use Case: Cleansing temporary construction datums created on-the-fly during automated routines.

question: How do you programmatically configure Drawing Section Views (Cross-Sections) in Creo?
answer:
Cross-section views reveal internal geometry in automated drawing packages.

Workflow:

  1. Create 3D Section in Solid: Ensure the 3D solid model contains a defined cross section (planar or offset) using ProXsecCreate() or verify via ProSolidXsecVisit().
  2. Apply to Drawing View: Retrieve the target drawing view using ProDrawingViewVisit().
  3. Configure Section Display: Call ProDrawingViewSectionSet() attaching the 3D model cross-section identifier to the designated drawing view.
  4. Control Hatch Patterns: Use ProDrawingXsecHatchVisit() and ProDrawingXsecHatchScaleSet() to adjust hatch angles, spacings, and materials according to corporate drafting standards.
  5. Regenerate: Invoke ProDrawingViewRegenerate() to render the cut face.

question: What are the common pitfalls and best practices for writing production-grade Creo customization software?
answer:
Developing industrial-grade Creo software requires addressing specific real-world operational challenges.

Best Practices Summary:

  • Model Regeneration Discipline: Avoid calling ProSolidRegenerate() inside tight loops; regenerate only once after batch element modifications are complete.
  • Pointer & Array Sanitization: Always free every ProArray, ProSelection, and ProWstring. Never leave orphan pointers in long-running Creo sessions.
  • Handle Regeneration Failures: Never assume geometry creation succeeds. Always check ProError return codes and implement graceful recovery handlers.
  • Windchill Workspace Awareness: Verify write-access and checkout status before calling save functions on enterprise parts.
  • Path & Unicode Portability: Use Creo-standard buffer sizes (PRO_PATH_SIZE, PRO_NAME_SIZE) and ProWstring to guarantee multi-byte international support across global design teams.
